rows.stem: If \(\begin{bmatrix} a & c & 0 \\ b & d & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) is a scalar matrix, then the value of \(a + 2b + 3c + 4d\) is :
rows.solution: A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are all equal, so every off-diagonal entry must be zero and the three diagonal entries must agree. Reading off \(\begin{bmatrix} a & c & 0 \\ b & d & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), the off-diagonal positions force \(c = 0\) and \(b = 0\), while the equal-diagonal condition forces \(a = d = 5\). Hence \(a + 2b + 3c + 4d = 5 + 2(0) + 3(0) + 4(5) = 25\), which is option 25.

rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.stem: Given that \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), matrix A is :
rows.solution: Since \(A = (A^{-1})^{-1}\), we simply invert the matrix we are given. Writing \(M = A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), we have \(\det M = \dfrac{1}{49}\big(2 \times 2 - 1 \times (-3)\big) = \dfrac{7}{49} = \dfrac{1}{7}\) and \(\operatorname{adj} M = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). Therefore \(A = M^{-1} = \dfrac{\operatorname{adj} M}{\det M} = 7 \times \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). As a check, \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \times \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = I\). So the answer is option \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\), then the value of \(I - A + A^2 - A^3 + \ldots\) is :
rows.solution: The series looks infinite, but this particular matrix is nilpotent. \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 4 & 2 - 2 \\ -8 + 8 & -4 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), so every term from \(A^2\) onwards vanishes and the sum collapses to just \(I - A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), which is option \(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 5 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), then the value of \(|\,A\,(\text{adj. }A)\,|\) is :
rows.solution: For any square matrix of order n, \(A\,(\text{adj. }A) = |A|\,I_n\); here \(n = 3\), so \(|A\,(\text{adj. }A)| = \big||A|\,I_3\big| = |A|^3\). Expanding along the first row, which conveniently has two zeros, \(|A| = -2\big(2(-1) - 3(1)\big) = -2(-2 - 3) = -2(-5) = 10\). Hence \(|A\,(\text{adj. }A)| = 10^3 = 1000\), which is option 1000. Note also that the question asks for a determinant, which is a number, so the two matrix-valued options 100 I and 10 I could not have been right in any case.

rows.stem: Given that \([1 \quad x]\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = 0\), the value of \(x\) is :
rows.solution: Carrying out the multiplication, \([1 \quad x]\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = [\,4 - 2x \quad 0\,]\). For this row matrix to be the zero matrix we need \(4 - 2x = 0\), so \(x = 2\), which is option 2.

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
rows.stem: Derivative of \(e^{2x}\) with respect to \(e^{x}\), is :
rows.solution: The derivative of one function with respect to another is the ratio of their derivatives with respect to the common variable. So \(\dfrac{d(e^{2x})}{d(e^{x})} = \dfrac{d(e^{2x})/dx}{d(e^{x})/dx} = \dfrac{2e^{2x}}{e^{x}} = 2e^{x}\), which is option \(2e^{x}\).

rows.stem:
For what value of k, the function given below is continuous at \(x = 0\) ?

\(f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sqrt{4+x} - 2}{x}, & x \neq 0 \\ k, & x = 0 \end{cases}\)
rows.solution: Continuity at \(x = 0\) requires the value there to equal the limit, i.e. \(k = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sqrt{4 + x} - 2}{x}\). That limit is of the indeterminate form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\), so rationalise the numerator: \(\dfrac{\sqrt{4 + x} - 2}{x} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{4 + x} + 2}{\sqrt{4 + x} + 2} = \dfrac{(4 + x) - 4}{x\left(\sqrt{4 + x} + 2\right)} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4 + x} + 2}\). Letting \(x \to 0\) gives \(\dfrac{1}{2 + 2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\). Hence \(k = \dfrac{1}{4}\), which is option \(\dfrac{1}{4}\).

rows.subtopic: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem
rows.stem: The value of \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{9 - x^2}}\) is :
rows.solution: Use the standard form \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}} = \sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{a} + c\) with \(a = 3\). Then \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{9 - x^2}} = \left[\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3}\right]_{0}^{3} = \sin^{-1}(1) - \sin^{-1}(0) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), which is option \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

rows.stem: The general solution of the differential equation \(x\,dy + y\,dx = 0\) is :
rows.solution: The left-hand side is already an exact differential: \(x\,dy + y\,dx = d(xy)\). So \(d(xy) = 0\), and integrating gives \(xy = c\), which is option \(xy = c\). Separating the variables leads to the same place: \(\dfrac{dy}{y} = -\dfrac{dx}{x}\) integrates to \(\log|y| = -\log|x| + \log|c|\), i.e. \(xy = c\).

rows.stem: The integrating factor of the differential equation \((x + 2y^2)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y\ (y > 0)\) is :
rows.solution: As written the equation is not linear in y, but it is linear in x, so treat x as the dependent variable. Inverting, \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{x + 2y^2}{y} = \dfrac{x}{y} + 2y\), that is \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} - \dfrac{1}{y}\,x = 2y\). This has the standard linear form with \(P(y) = -\dfrac{1}{y}\), so the integrating factor is \(e^{\int -\frac{1}{y}\,dy} = e^{-\log y} = \dfrac{1}{y}\), using \(y > 0\) to drop the modulus. That is option \(\dfrac{1}{y}\).

rows.stem: If \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are two vectors such that \(|\vec{a}| = 1\), \(|\vec{b}| = 2\) and \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \sqrt{3}\), then the angle between \(2\vec{a}\) and \(-\vec{b}\) is :
rows.solution: First find the angle between \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) themselves. From \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta\) we get \(\sqrt{3} = (1)(2)\cos\theta\), so \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\). Now multiplying \(\vec{a}\) by the positive scalar 2 does not change its direction at all, while replacing \(\vec{b}\) by \(-\vec{b}\) reverses it. So the angle between \(2\vec{a}\) and \(-\vec{b}\) is the supplement of \(\theta\), namely \(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\), which is option \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\).

rows.stem: The vectors \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{c} = -3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\) represents the sides of
rows.solution: First confirm the three vectors really do close up into a triangle: \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = (2 + 1 - 3)\hat{i} + (-1 - 3 + 4)\hat{j} + (1 - 5 + 4)\hat{k} = \vec{0}\), so taken in order they form a closed figure. Their squared lengths are \(|\vec{a}|^2 = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6\), \(|\vec{b}|^2 = 1 + 9 + 25 = 35\) and \(|\vec{c}|^2 = 9 + 16 + 16 = 41\). Since \(6 + 35 = 41\), the three sides satisfy the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, so the triangle is right-angled, matching the choice “a right-angled triangle”. It is neither equilateral nor isosceles, since \(\sqrt{6}\), \(\sqrt{35}\) and \(\sqrt{41}\) are all different.

rows.stem: Let \(\vec{a}\) be any vector such that \(|\vec{a}| = a\). The value of \(|\vec{a} \times \hat{i}|^{2} + |\vec{a} \times \hat{j}|^{2} + |\vec{a} \times \hat{k}|^{2}\) is :
rows.solution: Write \(\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}\), so that \(a^2 = a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2\). Crossing with a unit coordinate vector kills the component along that axis: \(\vec{a} \times \hat{i} = a_3\hat{j} - a_2\hat{k}\), so \(|\vec{a} \times \hat{i}|^2 = a_2^2 + a_3^2\). In the same way \(|\vec{a} \times \hat{j}|^2 = a_1^2 + a_3^2\) and \(|\vec{a} \times \hat{k}|^2 = a_1^2 + a_2^2\). Adding the three, each squared component appears exactly twice, so the total is \(2(a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2) = 2a^2\), which is option \(2a^2\).

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: The vector equation of a line passing through the point \((1, -1, 0)\) and parallel to Y-axis is :
rows.solution: A line parallel to the Y-axis has direction vector \(\hat{j}\), and the point \((1, -1, 0)\) has position vector \(\hat{i} - \hat{j}\). Using \(\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}\), the line is \(\vec{r} = (\hat{i} - \hat{j}) + \lambda\hat{j}\), which is option \(\vec{r} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \lambda\hat{j}\). The option \(\vec{r} = \lambda\hat{j}\) has the right direction but passes through the origin rather than through \((1, -1, 0)\).

rows.stem: The lines \(\dfrac{1-x}{2} = \dfrac{y-1}{3} = \dfrac{z}{1}\) and \(\dfrac{2x-3}{2p} = \dfrac{y}{-1} = \dfrac{z-4}{7}\) are perpendicular to each other for p equal to :
rows.solution: Put each line into standard symmetric form before reading off direction ratios, since both are disguised. The first, \(\dfrac{1 - x}{2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{3} = \dfrac{z}{1}\), becomes \(\dfrac{x - 1}{-2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{3} = \dfrac{z}{1}\), with direction ratios \(\langle -2,\ 3,\ 1 \rangle\). In the second, \(\dfrac{2x - 3}{2p} = \dfrac{2\left(x - \frac{3}{2}\right)}{2p} = \dfrac{x - \frac{3}{2}}{p}\), so its direction ratios are \(\langle p,\ -1,\ 7 \rangle\). The lines are perpendicular exactly when these have zero dot product: \((-2)(p) + (3)(-1) + (1)(7) = 0\), i.e. \(-2p + 4 = 0\), so \(p = 2\), which is option 2.

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem: The maximum value of \(Z = 4x + y\) for a L.P.P. whose feasible region is given below is :
rows.figure: REQUIRED - the feasible region is only given as a printed graph; the stem states no constraints. Corner points read off the marking scheme's clearer reproduction: O(0, 0), A(0, 50), B(20, 30), C(30, 0). Page idx 10 (marking scheme ms/p04.png shows the same graph legibly).
rows.solution: For a bounded feasible region the objective function attains its maximum at one of the corner points, so all that is needed is to test them. Reading the shaded region off the graph, its corners are \(O(0, 0)\), \(A(0, 50)\), \(B(20, 30)\) and \(C(30, 0)\). Evaluating \(Z = 4x + y\) at each: \(Z(O) = 0\), \(Z(A) = 4(0) + 50 = 50\), \(Z(B) = 4(20) + 30 = 110\) and \(Z(C) = 4(30) + 0 = 120\). The largest of these is 120, so the maximum value of Z is 120, which is option 120. The distractors 50 and 110 are precisely the values at the other two corners, so it is worth checking every corner rather than stopping at the first plausible one.

rows.stem:
The probability distribution of a random variable X is :

| X | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P(X) | 0.1 | k | 2k | k | 0.1 |

where k is some unknown constant.

The probability that the random variable X takes the value 2 is :
rows.solution: The probabilities in a probability distribution must add up to 1, which is what fixes k. Here \(0.1 + k + 2k + k + 0.1 = 1\), so \(4k = 0.8\) and \(k = 0.2\). The value asked for is \(P(X = 2) = 2k = 0.4 = \dfrac{2}{5}\), which is option \(\dfrac{2}{5}\). Note the question wants \(2k\), not k itself — \(k = \dfrac{1}{5}\) is the distractor.

rows.stem: The function \(f(x) = kx - \sin x\) is strictly increasing for
rows.solution: Differentiating, \(f'(x) = k - \cos x\). For f to be strictly increasing we need \(f'(x) > 0\) for every real x, i.e. \(k > \cos x\) for every x. Since \(\cos x\) takes every value in \([-1, 1]\), and in particular attains its largest value 1, this holds precisely when k exceeds 1. Hence \(k > 1\), which is option \(k > 1\). The option \(k > -1\) is not enough: at \(k = 0\), for instance, \(f(x) = -\sin x\) is decreasing on \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The relation \(R = \{(x, y) : (x + y)\) is a prime number and \(x, y \in N\}\) is not a reflexive relation.

**Reason (R) :** The number '2n' is composite for all natural numbers n.
rows.context: Questions No. 19 & 20, are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) based questions carrying 1 mark each. Two statements are given, one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and the Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Test the two statements separately. The Assertion: R is reflexive only if \((x, x) \in R\) for every natural number x, that is, only if \(x + x = 2x\) is a prime number for every x. This fails immediately — for \(x = 2\) we get \(2x = 4\), which is not prime, so \((2, 2) \notin R\) and R is not reflexive. The Assertion is TRUE. The Reason: it claims \(2n\) is composite for all natural numbers n, but at \(n = 1\) we get \(2n = 2\), which is prime, not composite. So the Reason is FALSE. Assertion true and Reason false gives the option Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false. The same value \(n = 1\) is worth noticing on both sides: it is exactly why \((1, 1)\) does belong to R, since \(1 + 1 = 2\) is prime. R fails reflexivity because of the other natural numbers, not because of that one.

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The corner points of the bounded feasible region of a L.P.P. are shown below. The maximum value of \(Z = x + 2y\) occurs at infinite points.

**Reason (R) :** The optimal solution of a LPP having bounded feasible region must occur at corner points.
rows.context: Questions No. 19 & 20, are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) based questions carrying 1 mark each. Two statements are given, one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and the Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.figure: REQUIRED - the Assertion is ABOUT a printed shaded feasible region; no corner points are given in the text. Corner points read off the marking scheme's clearer reproduction: S(40, 20), R(60, 30), P(60, 0), Q(120, 0), with lines through N(0, 60) and T(120, 60). Page idx 12 (marking scheme ms/p05.png shows the same graph legibly).
rows.solution: Take the Assertion first. The corner points of the shaded bounded region are \(S(40, 20)\), \(R(60, 30)\), \(Q(120, 0)\) and \(P(60, 0)\). Evaluating \(Z = x + 2y\): \(Z(S) = 40 + 40 = 80\), \(Z(R) = 60 + 60 = 120\), \(Z(Q) = 120 + 0 = 120\) and \(Z(P) = 60 + 0 = 60\). The maximum value 120 is attained at TWO distinct corner points, R and Q. When a linear objective takes the same optimal value at two corner points it takes that value at every point of the segment joining them, so the maximum occurs at infinitely many points and the Assertion is TRUE. The Reason is also a TRUE statement — for a bounded feasible region the optimal value is always attained at a corner point (possibly elsewhere as well). But it does not explain the Assertion: it only says an optimum occurs at a corner, whereas what produces infinitely many optimal points here is the two corners happening to share the same value. So both are true and the Reason is not the correct explanation, giving the option Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

rows.stem: Express \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x}\right)\), where \(\dfrac{-\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) in the simplest form.
rows.solution: The trick is to convert to half-angles, because that makes the numerator and denominator share a common factor. Using \(\cos x = \cos^2\dfrac{x}{2} - \sin^2\dfrac{x}{2}\) and \(1 - \sin x = \left(\cos\dfrac{x}{2} - \sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2\), the fraction becomes \(\dfrac{\left(\cos\frac{x}{2} - \sin\frac{x}{2}\right)\left(\cos\frac{x}{2} + \sin\frac{x}{2}\right)}{\left(\cos\frac{x}{2} - \sin\frac{x}{2}\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{\cos\frac{x}{2} + \sin\frac{x}{2}}{\cos\frac{x}{2} - \sin\frac{x}{2}}\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\) gives \(\dfrac{1 + \tan\frac{x}{2}}{1 - \tan\frac{x}{2}}\), which is exactly the expansion of \(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\) since \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\). Hence \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{x}{2}\). The last step is legitimate because for \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) the angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{x}{2}\) lies in \(\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), which is inside the principal branch \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) of \(\tan^{-1}\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: Find the principal value of \(\tan^{-1}(1) + \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\).
rows.solution: Evaluate each inverse function on its own principal branch, being careful with the two negative arguments. First, \(\tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Second, \(\cos^{-1}\) has principal range \([0, \pi]\) and satisfies \(\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}(x)\), so \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \pi - \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Third, \(\sin^{-1}\) is an odd function, so \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Adding the three, \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Note how the first and third terms cancel exactly, leaving the principal value \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).

rows.stem: If \(y = \cos^{3}(\sec^{2} 2t)\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}\).
rows.solution: This is a three-layer composite, so peel it from the outside in with the chain rule. Writing \(y = \left[\cos(\sec^{2} 2t)\right]^{3}\), the outer power gives \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 3\cos^{2}(\sec^{2} 2t) \times \left[-\sin(\sec^{2} 2t)\right] \times \dfrac{d(\sec^{2} 2t)}{dt}\). For the innermost derivative, \(\dfrac{d(\sec^{2} 2t)}{dt} = 2\sec 2t \times \dfrac{d(\sec 2t)}{dt} = 2\sec 2t \times \left(\sec 2t \tan 2t \times 2\right) = 4\sec^{2} 2t \tan 2t\). Substituting this back, \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -3\cos^{2}(\sec^{2} 2t)\,\sin(\sec^{2} 2t) \times 4\sec^{2} 2t \tan 2t\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -12\cos^{2}(\sec^{2} 2t)\,\sin(\sec^{2} 2t)\,\sec^{2} 2t\,\tan 2t\).

rows.stem: If \(x^{y} = e^{x-y}\), prove that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\log x}{(1 + \log x)^{2}}\).
rows.solution: Take logarithms of both sides first, which brings the variable exponent down and makes the relation manageable. From \(x^{y} = e^{x - y}\) we get \(\log\left(x^{y}\right) = \log\left(e^{x-y}\right)\), i.e. \(y\log x = (x - y)\log e = x - y\). Collecting the y terms on one side, \(y\log x + y = x\), so \(y(1 + \log x) = x\) and \(y = \dfrac{x}{1 + \log x}\). This explicit form is much easier to differentiate than the original implicit one. By the quotient rule, \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{(1 + \log x)(1) - x\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)}{(1 + \log x)^{2}} = \dfrac{1 + \log x - 1}{(1 + \log x)^{2}} = \dfrac{\log x}{(1 + \log x)^{2}}\), which is what we were asked to prove.

rows.stem: Find the interval in which the function \(f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{3} + 10\) is strictly decreasing.
rows.solution: Differentiating, \(f'(x) = 4x^{3} - 12x^{2} = 4x^{2}(x - 3)\). The factor \(4x^{2}\) is never negative, so the sign of \(f'\) is decided entirely by the factor \(x - 3\): we get \(f'(x) < 0\) for every \(x < 3\) apart from \(x = 0\), where \(f'(0) = 0\). Since that stationary point is a single isolated point, the function goes on falling straight through it, so f is strictly decreasing all the way up to \(x = 3\). The marking scheme accepts either way of recording this: \((-\infty, 0) \cup (0, 3)\), which leaves the stationary point out, or \((-\infty, 0] \cup [0, 3]\), which is just \((-\infty, 3]\) written in two pieces. Beyond \(x = 3\) the derivative is positive, so the function increases there.

rows.stem: The volume of a cube is increasing at the rate of 6 cm\(^{3}\)/s. How fast is the surface area of cube increasing, when the length of an edge is 8 cm ?
rows.solution: Let the edge of the cube be x cm at time t. The volume is \(V = x^{3}\), so differentiating with respect to t, \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 3x^{2}\dfrac{dx}{dt}\). We are told \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 6\) cm\(^{3}\)/s, which gives \(6 = 3x^{2}\dfrac{dx}{dt}\), so \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{2}{x^{2}}\) cm/s. The surface area is \(S = 6x^{2}\), so \(\dfrac{dS}{dt} = 12x\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 12x \times \dfrac{2}{x^{2}} = \dfrac{24}{x}\). Putting \(x = 8\), \(\dfrac{dS}{dt} = \dfrac{24}{8} = 3\). So the surface area is increasing at the rate of 3 cm\(^{2}\)/s when the edge is 8 cm.

rows.stem: Find : \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{x(x^{2} - 1)}\,dx\).
rows.solution: Partial fractions would work, but there is a quicker substitution suggested by pulling \(x^{3}\) out of the denominator. Write \(x(x^{2} - 1) = x^{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)\), so that \(I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{x^{3}\left(1 - \frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\left(\frac{2}{x^{3}}\right)dx}{1 - \frac{1}{x^{2}}}\). Now put \(t = 1 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\), for which \(dt = \dfrac{2}{x^{3}}\,dx\) — exactly the numerator we arranged. The integral becomes \(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\log|t| + c = \dfrac{1}{2}\log\left|1 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right| + c\), which may equally be written \(\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left|\dfrac{x^{2} - 1}{x^{2}}\right| + c\). Checking by differentiation: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2x}{x^{2} - 1} - \dfrac{2}{x}\right) = \dfrac{x}{x^{2} - 1} - \dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{x^{2} - (x^{2} - 1)}{x(x^{2} - 1)} = \dfrac{1}{x(x^{2} - 1)}\), as required.

rows.stem: Given that \(y = (\sin x)^{x} \cdot x^{\sin x} + a^{x}\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).
rows.solution: Split y into the part that needs logarithmic differentiation and the part that does not. Put \(u = (\sin x)^{x} \cdot x^{\sin x}\), so that \(y = u + a^{x}\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{du}{dx} + a^{x}\log a\). For u, both factors have a variable in the exponent, so take logarithms: \(\log u = x\log(\sin x) + \sin x \cdot \log x\). Differentiating both sides with respect to x, and using the product rule on each term on the right, \(\dfrac{1}{u}\dfrac{du}{dx} = \left[\log(\sin x) + x \cdot \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\right] + \left[\dfrac{\sin x}{x} + \cos x \cdot \log x\right]\). Hence \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = (\sin x)^{x}\,x^{\sin x}\left[\log(\sin x) + x\cot x + \dfrac{\sin x}{x} + \cos x \log x\right]\), and therefore \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = (\sin x)^{x}\,x^{\sin x}\left[\log(\sin x) + x\cot x + \dfrac{\sin x}{x} + \cos x \log x\right] + a^{x}\log a\).

rows.stem: Evaluate : \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{x\,dx}{1 + \cos 2x + \sin 2x}\)
rows.solution: The x in the numerator is what makes this hard, so use the king property \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) to eliminate it. Replacing x by \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\) turns \(\cos 2x\) into \(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 2x\right) = \sin 2x\) and \(\sin 2x\) into \(\cos 2x\), so the denominator is left unchanged and \(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\frac{\pi}{4} - x}{1 + \cos 2x + \sin 2x}\,dx\). Adding this to the original expression for I, the x terms cancel: \(2I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \cos 2x + \sin 2x}\). Now simplify the denominator using \(1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^{2}x\) and \(\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x\): it becomes \(2\cos^{2}x + 2\sin x\cos x = 2\left(\cos^{2}x + \sin x\cos x\right)\). So \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{16}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{dx}{\cos^{2}x + \sin x\cos x}\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(\cos^{2}x\) gives \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{16}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\sec^{2}x\,dx}{1 + \tan x}\), and substituting \(t = 1 + \tan x\) (so \(dt = \sec^{2}x\,dx\)) makes it a logarithm: \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{16}\Big[\log|1 + \tan x|\Big]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \dfrac{\pi}{16}(\log 2 - \log 1) = \dfrac{\pi}{16}\log 2\).

rows.stem: Find : \(\displaystyle\int e^{x}\left[\dfrac{1}{(1 + x^{2})^{3/2}} + \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}\right] dx\)
rows.solution: This is the standard form \(\displaystyle\int e^{x}\big(f(x) + f'(x)\big)\,dx = e^{x}f(x) + c\); the only work is spotting which bracketed term is f and which is \(f'\). Try \(f(x) = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}\), the second term. By the quotient rule, \(f'(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}} - x \cdot \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}}{1 + x^{2}} = \dfrac{(1 + x^{2}) - x^{2}}{(1 + x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{(1 + x^{2})^{3/2}}\), which is precisely the first term in the bracket. So the integrand is \(e^{x}\big(f(x) + f'(x)\big)\) and \(I = e^{x}\,\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}} + c\).

rows.stem: Find : \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{3x + 5}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 2x + 4}}\,dx\)
rows.solution:
The numerator is split into a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic under the root, plus a constant. Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^2 + 2x + 4\right) = 2x + 2\), write \(3x + 5 = \frac{3}{2}(2x + 2) + 2\), which is an identity because \(\frac{3}{2}(2x + 2) = 3x + 3\) and \(3 + 2 = 5\).
Hence \(I = \frac{3}{2}\int \frac{2x + 2}{\sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4}}\,dx + 2\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4}}\).
In the first integral put \(t = x^2 + 2x + 4\), so that \(dt = (2x + 2)\,dx\) and it becomes \(\frac{3}{2}\int t^{-1/2}\,dt = \frac{3}{2}\left(2\sqrt{t}\right) = 3\sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4}\).
For the second, complete the square: \(x^2 + 2x + 4 = (x + 1)^2 + 3 = (x + 1)^2 + \left(\sqrt{3}\right)^2\). Using the standard result \(\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}} = \log\left|x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2}\right|\), this integral is \(2\log\left|(x + 1) + \sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4}\right|\).
Therefore \(I = 3\sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4} + 2\log\left|(x + 1) + \sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4}\right| + C\).
(Check by differentiating: the first term gives \(\frac{3(x + 1)}{\sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4}}\) and the second gives \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4}}\), and these add to \(\frac{3x + 5}{\sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 4}}\), the original integrand.)

rows.stem: Find the particular solution of the differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y \cot 2x\), given that \(y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 2\).
rows.solution:
The variables separate at once: \(\frac{dy}{y} = \cot 2x\,dx\).
Integrating both sides, \(\int \frac{dy}{y} = \int \cot 2x\,dx\) gives \(\log|y| = \frac{1}{2}\log|\sin 2x| + \log c\), where the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) comes from the \(2x\) inside the cotangent.
Combining the right-hand side into a single logarithm, \(\log|y| = \log\left(c\sqrt{|\sin 2x|}\right)\), so the general solution is \(y = c\sqrt{\sin 2x}\).
Now use the given condition. At \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\) we have \(\sin 2x = \sin \frac{\pi}{2} = 1\), so \(y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = 2\) gives \(2 = c\sqrt{1} = c\).
Hence the required particular solution is \(y = 2\sqrt{\sin 2x}\).

rows.stem: Find the particular solution of the differential equation \(\left(xe^{y/x} + y\right) dx = x\,dy\), given that \(y = 1\) when \(x = 1\).
rows.solution:
Rearranging, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{xe^{y/x} + y}{x} = e^{y/x} + \frac{y}{x}\). The right-hand side depends on \(x\) and \(y\) only through the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\), so the equation is homogeneous.
Put \(y = vx\), so that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\). Substituting gives \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = e^{v} + v\), and the \(v\) cancels from both sides to leave \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = e^{v}\).
This separates as \(e^{-v}\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}\). Integrating, \(-e^{-v} = \log|x| + C\), and restoring \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) gives \(-e^{-y/x} = \log|x| + C\).
Apply \(y = 1\) when \(x = 1\): \(-e^{-1} = \log 1 + C = C\), so \(C = -e^{-1}\).
The particular solution is therefore \(-e^{-y/x} = \log|x| - e^{-1}\), which is usually written \(\log|x| + e^{-y/x} = e^{-1}\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following linear programming problem graphically :

Maximise \(Z = 2x + 3y\)

subject to the constraints :

\(x + y \le 6\)

\(x \ge 2\)

\(y \le 3\)

\(x, y \ge 0\)
rows.solution:
Draw the lines \(x + y = 6\), \(x = 2\) and \(y = 3\), and shade the region satisfying every constraint together with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\). The feasible region is the bounded quadrilateral ABCD with corner points \(A(2, 3)\), \(B(3, 3)\), \(C(6, 0)\) and \(D(2, 0)\): A is where \(x = 2\) meets \(y = 3\), B is where \(y = 3\) meets \(x + y = 6\), C is where \(x + y = 6\) meets the X-axis, and D is where \(x = 2\) meets the X-axis.
Evaluate \(Z = 2x + 3y\) at each corner point:

| Corner point | Value of \(Z = 2x + 3y\) |
|---|---|
| \(A(2, 3)\) | \(4 + 9 = 13\) |
| \(B(3, 3)\) | \(6 + 9 = 15\) |
| \(C(6, 0)\) | \(12 + 0 = 12\) |
| \(D(2, 0)\) | \(4 + 0 = 4\) |

The feasible region is bounded, so the objective function attains its maximum at one of the corner points. The largest of the four values is \(15\).
Hence the maximum value of \(Z\) is \(15\), occurring at \(x = 3\), \(y = 3\).

rows.stem: A card from a well shuffled deck of 52 playing cards is lost. From the remaining cards of the pack, a card is drawn at random and is found to be a King. Find the probability of the lost card being a King.
rows.solution:
Let \(E_1\) be the event that the lost card is a King and \(E_2\) the event that it is not, and let A be the event that a card drawn from the remaining \(51\) cards is a King. A pack contains \(4\) Kings among \(52\) cards, so \(P(E_1) = \frac{4}{52} = \frac{1}{13}\) and \(P(E_2) = \frac{48}{52} = \frac{12}{13}\).
If the lost card was a King, only \(3\) Kings remain among the \(51\), so \(P(A\,|\,E_1) = \frac{3}{51}\). If it was not a King, all \(4\) Kings remain, so \(P(A\,|\,E_2) = \frac{4}{51}\).
We are told the drawn card is a King and asked for the probability that the lost one was, so this is Bayes' theorem: \(P(E_1\,|\,A) = \frac{P(E_1)P(A\,|\,E_1)}{P(E_1)P(A\,|\,E_1) + P(E_2)P(A\,|\,E_2)}\).
Substituting, \(P(E_1\,|\,A) = \frac{\frac{1}{13} \times \frac{3}{51}}{\frac{1}{13} \times \frac{3}{51} + \frac{12}{13} \times \frac{4}{51}}\). The common factor \(\frac{1}{13 \times 51}\) cancels from numerator and denominator, leaving \(\frac{3}{3 + 48} = \frac{3}{51} = \frac{1}{17}\).
So the probability that the lost card was a King is \(\frac{1}{17}\).
(This is slightly less than the prior probability \(\frac{1}{13}\), which is as it should be: a King is harder to draw when a King has already been lost, so drawing one is mild evidence against \(E_1\).)

rows.stem: A biased die is twice as likely to show an even number as an odd number. If such a die is thrown twice, find the probability distribution of the number of sixes. Also, find the mean of the distribution.
rows.solution:
Let each odd face carry probability \(p\). The die being twice as likely to show an even number as an odd number makes each even face carry probability \(2p\). The six probabilities must add to \(1\), so \(3p + 3(2p) = 9p = 1\), giving \(p = \frac{1}{9}\).
Six is an even face, so \(P(\text{six}) = 2p = \frac{2}{9}\) and \(P(\text{not a six}) = \frac{7}{9}\).
Let X be the number of sixes obtained in the two throws, so X takes the values \(0\), \(1\) and \(2\), and the throws are independent. Then \(P(X = 0) = \frac{7}{9} \times \frac{7}{9} = \frac{49}{81}\), \(P(X = 1) = 2 \times \frac{7}{9} \times \frac{2}{9} = \frac{28}{81}\) (the factor \(2\) because the six may fall on either throw), and \(P(X = 2) = \frac{2}{9} \times \frac{2}{9} = \frac{4}{81}\).
The probability distribution of the number of sixes is therefore

| \(X\) | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(P(X)\) | \(\frac{49}{81}\) | \(\frac{28}{81}\) | \(\frac{4}{81}\) |

(These add to \(\frac{49 + 28 + 4}{81} = 1\), as they must.)
The mean is \(\sum x_i p_i = 0\left(\frac{49}{81}\right) + 1\left(\frac{28}{81}\right) + 2\left(\frac{4}{81}\right) = \frac{28 + 8}{81} = \frac{36}{81} = \frac{4}{9}\).
So the mean of the distribution is \(\frac{4}{9}\). (X is binomial with \(n = 2\) and \(p = \frac{2}{9}\), and the check \(np = 2 \times \frac{2}{9} = \frac{4}{9}\) agrees.)

rows.stem: Sketch the graph of \(y = x\,|x|\) and hence find the area bounded by this curve, X-axis and the ordinates \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\), using integration.
rows.solution:
Since \(|x| = -x\) for \(x < 0\) and \(|x| = x\) for \(x \ge 0\), the curve is the piecewise parabola \(y = -x^2\) for \(x < 0\) and \(y = x^2\) for \(x \ge 0\).
Sketch: for \(x \ge 0\) it is the right-hand half of the parabola \(y = x^2\), rising through the origin to \((2, 4)\); for \(x < 0\) it is that arc reflected through the origin, falling to \((-2, -4)\). The graph passes through the origin, lies below the X-axis for \(x < 0\) and above it for \(x > 0\), and is symmetric about the origin.
Because the curve crosses the X-axis at \(x = 0\), the region must be split there and the two parts added as areas.
For \(0 \le x \le 2\) the curve lies above the axis, so that part has area \(\int_{0}^{2} x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = \frac{8}{3}\).
For \(-2 \le x \le 0\) the curve lies below the axis, so that part has area \(\int_{-2}^{0}(-y)\,dx = \int_{-2}^{0} x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{0} = 0 - \left(-\frac{8}{3}\right) = \frac{8}{3}\).
The two parts are congruent, each of area \(\frac{8}{3}\), so the required area is \(\frac{8}{3} + \frac{8}{3} = \frac{16}{3}\) square units.
[A note on the official marking scheme, which compresses all of this into \(\text{Area} = \int_{-2}^{2} y\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{2} y\,dx = \frac{16}{3}\). Read as areas — which is how its figure shades the region, both lobes together — that chain is fine and gives the same \(\frac{16}{3}\). But do not read it as an identity between signed integrals: \(y = x|x|\) is an odd function, so the signed \(\int_{-2}^{2} y\,dx\) is \(0\), and the rule \(\int_{-a}^{a} f = 2\int_{0}^{a} f\) holds for even functions, not odd ones. That is exactly why the region is split at the origin above. A student who integrates straight through and gets \(0\) has not made an arithmetic slip — they have integrated the signed function instead of measuring area.]

rows.subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
rows.stem: Using integration, find the area bounded by the ellipse \(9x^{2} + 25y^{2} = 225\), the lines \(x = -2\), \(x = 2\), and the X-axis.
rows.solution:
Divide \(9x^2 + 25y^2 = 225\) throughout by \(225\) to reach the standard form \(\frac{x^2}{25} + \frac{y^2}{9} = 1\). This is an ellipse centred at the origin with semi-axis \(a = 5\) along the X-axis and \(b = 3\) along the Y-axis, so \(y = \pm\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{25 - x^2}\).
The region bounded by the ellipse, the lines \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\) and the X-axis is the strip of the upper half of the ellipse standing between those two ordinates, so we take the positive root \(y = \frac{3}{5}\sqrt{5^2 - x^2}\). Both lines cut the curve, since \(2 < 5\).
Hence the required area is \(\int_{-2}^{2} \frac{3}{5}\sqrt{5^2 - x^2}\,dx\). This integrand is an even function of \(x\), so the integral equals \(\frac{6}{5}\int_{0}^{2}\sqrt{5^2 - x^2}\,dx\).
Using the standard result \(\int \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx = \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \frac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a}\) with \(a = 5\), the area is \(\frac{6}{5}\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{25 - x^2} + \frac{25}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{5}\right]_{0}^{2}\).
At \(x = 2\) the bracket equals \(1 \times \sqrt{21} + \frac{25}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{2}{5}\), and at \(x = 0\) it equals \(0\).
Therefore the area is \(\frac{6}{5}\left(\sqrt{21} + \frac{25}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{2}{5}\right) = \frac{6\sqrt{21}}{5} + 15\sin^{-1}\frac{2}{5}\) square units.
Numerically that is about \(5{\cdot}50 + 6{\cdot}17 = 11{\cdot}67\) square units, a plausible share of the upper half of the ellipse, whose area is \(\frac{1}{2}\pi ab = \frac{15\pi}{2} \approx 23{\cdot}56\) square units.

rows.stem: Let \(A = R - \{5\}\) and \(B = R - \{1\}\). Consider the function \(f : A \to B\), defined by \(f(x) = \dfrac{x-3}{x-5}\). Show that f is one-one and onto.
rows.solution:
One-one. Suppose \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) for some \(x_1, x_2 \in A\), that is \(\frac{x_1 - 3}{x_1 - 5} = \frac{x_2 - 3}{x_2 - 5}\). Cross-multiplying (legitimate, since neither denominator is zero on A), \((x_1 - 3)(x_2 - 5) = (x_2 - 3)(x_1 - 5)\), i.e. \(x_1x_2 - 5x_1 - 3x_2 + 15 = x_1x_2 - 5x_2 - 3x_1 + 15\).
Cancelling \(x_1x_2\) and \(15\) leaves \(-5x_1 - 3x_2 = -5x_2 - 3x_1\), so \(-2x_1 = -2x_2\) and hence \(x_1 = x_2\). Therefore f is one-one.
Onto. Let \(y \in B\) be arbitrary and try to solve \(y = \frac{x - 3}{x - 5}\) for \(x\). Then \(y(x - 5) = x - 3\), so \(yx - 5y = x - 3\), giving \(x(y - 1) = 5y - 3\) and \(x = \frac{5y - 3}{y - 1}\).
Since \(y \in B = R - \{1\}\) we have \(y \ne 1\), so this \(x\) is a well-defined real number. It also lies in A: were \(\frac{5y - 3}{y - 1}\) equal to \(5\) we would need \(5y - 3 = 5y - 5\), i.e. \(-3 = -5\), which is impossible, so \(x \ne 5\).
This \(x\) does map to \(y\): \(f\left(\frac{5y - 3}{y - 1}\right) = \frac{\frac{5y - 3}{y - 1} - 3}{\frac{5y - 3}{y - 1} - 5} = \frac{(5y - 3) - 3(y - 1)}{(5y - 3) - 5(y - 1)} = \frac{2y}{2} = y\).
So every element of B has a pre-image in A, and f is onto. Being both one-one and onto, f is a bijection from A to B.

rows.stem: Check whether the relation S in the set of real numbers R defined by \(S = \{(a, b) : \text{where } a - b + \sqrt{2} \text{ is an irrational number}\}\) is reflexive, symmetric or transitive.
rows.solution:
Reflexive. For any real number a, \(a - a + \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2}\), which is irrational. So \((a, a) \in S\) for every \(a \in R\), and S is reflexive.
Symmetric. Take \(a = \sqrt{2}\) and \(b = 1\). Then \(a - b + \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2} - 1 + \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2} - 1\), which is irrational, so \(\left(\sqrt{2},\, 1\right) \in S\). Reversing the pair, \(b - a + \sqrt{2} = 1 - \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} = 1\), which is rational, so \(\left(1,\, \sqrt{2}\right) \notin S\). A single counter-example suffices: S is not symmetric.
Transitive. Take \(a = 1\), \(b = \sqrt{3}\) and \(c = \sqrt{2}\). Then \(a - b + \sqrt{2} = 1 - \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2}\) is irrational, so \(\left(1,\, \sqrt{3}\right) \in S\), and \(b - c + \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{3}\) is irrational, so \(\left(\sqrt{3},\, \sqrt{2}\right) \in S\). But \(a - c + \sqrt{2} = 1 - \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} = 1\) is rational, so \(\left(1,\, \sqrt{2}\right) \notin S\). Hence S is not transitive.
Therefore S is reflexive, but neither symmetric nor transitive.

rows.stem:
If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), find \(A^{-1}\) and hence solve the following system of equations :

\(2x + y - 3z = 13\)

\(3x + 2y + z = 4\)

\(x + 2y - z = 8\)
rows.solution:
First confirm that A can be inverted. Expanding the determinant along the first row,
\(|A| = 2\left[(2)(-1) - (1)(2)\right] - 1\left[(3)(-1) - (1)(1)\right] + (-3)\left[(3)(2) - (2)(1)\right] = 2(-4) - 1(-4) - 3(4) = -8 + 4 - 12 = -16\).
Since \(|A| = -16 \ne 0\), \(A^{-1}\) exists.
The cofactors of A are \(A_{11} = -4\), \(A_{12} = 4\), \(A_{13} = 4\), \(A_{21} = -5\), \(A_{22} = 1\), \(A_{23} = -3\), \(A_{31} = 7\), \(A_{32} = -11\) and \(A_{33} = 1\). The adjoint is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors, so \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -5 & 7 \\ 4 & 1 & -11 \\ 4 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Hence \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A = -\frac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -4 & -5 & 7 \\ 4 & 1 & -11 \\ 4 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
The coefficient matrix of the three equations is exactly A, so the system is \(AX = B\) with \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 13 \\ 4 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}\), and since \(A^{-1}\) exists the unique solution is \(X = A^{-1}B\).
Carrying out the multiplication, \(X = -\frac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -4 & -5 & 7 \\ 4 & 1 & -11 \\ 4 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 13 \\ 4 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -52 - 20 + 56 \\ 52 + 4 - 88 \\ 52 - 12 + 8 \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -16 \\ -32 \\ 48 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}\).
Hence \(x = 1\), \(y = 2\) and \(z = -3\).
(Substituting back: \(2 + 2 + 9 = 13\), \(3 + 4 - 3 = 4\) and \(1 + 4 + 3 = 8\), so all three equations are satisfied.)

rows.stem: Find the distance between the line \(\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{2y-6}{4} = \dfrac{1-z}{-1}\) and another line parallel to it passing through the point \((4, 0, -5)\).
rows.solution:
First rewrite the given line in standard symmetric form. Since \(\frac{2y - 6}{4} = \frac{2(y - 3)}{4} = \frac{y - 3}{2}\) and \(\frac{1 - z}{-1} = \frac{-(z - 1)}{-1} = \frac{z - 1}{1}\), the line is \(L_1 : \frac{x - 0}{2} = \frac{y - 3}{2} = \frac{z - 1}{1}\). So \(L_1\) passes through \(A_1(0, 3, 1)\) and has direction \(\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\).
The other line is parallel to it and passes through \(A_2(4, 0, -5)\), so \(L_2 : \frac{x - 4}{2} = \frac{y}{2} = \frac{z + 5}{1}\), with the same direction \(\vec{b}\).
For two parallel lines \(\vec{r} = \vec{a_1} + \lambda \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{r} = \vec{a_2} + \mu \vec{b}\), the distance between them is \(d = \frac{\left|\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right) \times \vec{b}\right|}{\left|\vec{b}\right|}\).
Here \(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1} = \left(4\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\right) - \left(0\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) = 4\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}\).
Then \(\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right) \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & -3 & -6 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(-3 + 12) - \hat{j}(4 + 12) + \hat{k}(8 + 6) = 9\hat{i} - 16\hat{j} + 14\hat{k}\).
Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{81 + 256 + 196} = \sqrt{533}\), while \(\left|\vec{b}\right| = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 1} = 3\).
Hence the distance between the two lines is \(\frac{\sqrt{533}}{3}\) units, which is about \(7{\cdot}70\) units.

rows.stem: If the lines \(\dfrac{x-1}{-3} = \dfrac{y-2}{2k} = \dfrac{z-3}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{x-1}{3k} = \dfrac{y-1}{1} = \dfrac{z-6}{-7}\) are perpendicular to each other, find the value of k and hence write the vector equation of a line perpendicular to these two lines and passing through the point \((3, -4, 7)\).
rows.solution:
The direction ratios are read off the denominators: \(L_1\) has direction \(-3,\ 2k,\ 2\) and \(L_2\) has direction \(3k,\ 1,\ -7\).
Two lines are perpendicular exactly when the dot product of their directions vanishes, so \((-3)(3k) + (2k)(1) + (2)(-7) = 0\), that is \(-9k + 2k - 14 = 0\), i.e. \(-7k = 14\), giving \(k = -2\).
With \(k = -2\) the two directions become \(\vec{b_1} = -3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b_2} = -6\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 7\hat{k}\). (Check: \((-3)(-6) + (-4)(1) + (2)(-7) = 18 - 4 - 14 = 0\), so they are indeed perpendicular.)
A line perpendicular to both must be along their cross product: \(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -3 & -4 & 2 \\ -6 & 1 & -7 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(28 - 2) - \hat{j}(21 + 12) + \hat{k}(-3 - 24) = 26\hat{i} - 33\hat{j} - 27\hat{k}\).
The required line passes through \((3, -4, 7)\), whose position vector is \(3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}\).
Hence its vector equation is \(\vec{r} = \left(3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}\right) + \lambda\left(26\hat{i} - 33\hat{j} - 27\hat{k}\right)\).

rows.stem: Determine the number of units (\(x\)) that should be sold to maximise the revenue \(R(x) = x\,p(x)\). Also, verify the result.
rows.context:
A store has been selling calculators at ₹ 350 each. A market survey indicates that a reduction in price (p) of calculator increases the number of units (\(x\)) sold. The relation between the price and quantity sold is given by the demand function \(p = 450 - \dfrac{1}{2}x\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figure: DECORATIVE - a clip-art picture of a calculator with a Rs 350 price tag. Every number the sub-parts need is in the passage text. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
The revenue from selling x units at price \(p(x)\) each is \(R(x) = x\,p(x) = x\left(450 - \frac{x}{2}\right) = 450x - \frac{x^2}{2}\).
Differentiating, \(\frac{dR}{dx} = 450 - x\). For a maximum or a minimum, \(\frac{dR}{dx} = 0\), which gives \(x = 450\).
To verify that this is a maximum, differentiate again: \(\frac{d^2R}{dx^2} = -1\), which is negative for every x and in particular at \(x = 450\). By the second derivative test the stationary point is a point of maximum.
Hence the revenue is maximised when \(450\) units are sold.
(The maximum revenue is then \(R(450) = 450(450) - \frac{450^2}{2} = 202500 - 101250 = 101250\) rupees.)

rows.stem: What rebate in price of calculator should the store give to maximise the revenue ?
rows.context:
A store has been selling calculators at ₹ 350 each. A market survey indicates that a reduction in price (p) of calculator increases the number of units (\(x\)) sold. The relation between the price and quantity sold is given by the demand function \(p = 450 - \dfrac{1}{2}x\).

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
From part (i) the revenue is greatest when \(x = 450\) units are sold, so we need the price at which that many units will sell.
The demand function gives it directly: \(p = 450 - \frac{x}{2} = 450 - \frac{450}{2} = 450 - 225 = 225\) rupees.
The calculators were being sold at \(350\) rupees each, so the reduction required is \(350 - 225 = 125\).
The store should therefore give a rebate of \(125\) rupees per calculator.

rows.stem: How far is the star V from star A ?
rows.context:
An instructor at the astronomical centre shows three among the brightest stars in a particular constellation. Assume that the telescope is located at O(0, 0, 0) and the three stars have their locations at the points D, A and V having position vectors \(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\), \(7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\) and \(-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}\) respectively.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figure: DECORATIVE - a night-sky photograph with the three stars labelled D, A and V and the telescope at O. Every position vector the sub-parts need is printed in the passage. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
The distance from star A to star V is the magnitude of \(\overrightarrow{AV}\), and \(\overrightarrow{AV}\) is the position vector of V minus the position vector of A.
So \(\overrightarrow{AV} = \left(-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}\right) - \left(7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\right) = -10\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\).
Hence \(\left|\overrightarrow{AV}\right| = \sqrt{(-10)^2 + 2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{100 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{113}\) units, which is about \(10{\cdot}63\) units.

rows.stem: Find a unit vector in the direction of \(\overrightarrow{DA}\).
rows.context:
An instructor at the astronomical centre shows three among the brightest stars in a particular constellation. Assume that the telescope is located at O(0, 0, 0) and the three stars have their locations at the points D, A and V having position vectors \(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\), \(7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\) and \(-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}\) respectively.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
First find the vector itself: \(\overrightarrow{DA}\) is the position vector of A minus the position vector of D, so \(\overrightarrow{DA} = \left(7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\right) - \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\right) = 5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\).
Its magnitude is \(\left|\overrightarrow{DA}\right| = \sqrt{5^2 + 2^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25 + 4 + 16} = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\).
A unit vector in the direction of a vector is the vector divided by its own magnitude, so the required unit vector is \(\frac{5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}}{3\sqrt{5}}\).

rows.stem: Find the measure of \(\angle VDA\).
rows.context:
An instructor at the astronomical centre shows three among the brightest stars in a particular constellation. Assume that the telescope is located at O(0, 0, 0) and the three stars have their locations at the points D, A and V having position vectors \(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\), \(7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\) and \(-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}\) respectively.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The angle \(\angle VDA\) has its vertex at D, so it is the angle between the vectors \(\overrightarrow{DV}\) and \(\overrightarrow{DA}\) — both must be taken as pointing away from D.
These are \(\overrightarrow{DV} = \left(-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}\right) - \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\right) = -5\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}\) and \(\overrightarrow{DA} = \left(7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\right) - \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\right) = 5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\).
Their dot product is \(\overrightarrow{DV} \cdot \overrightarrow{DA} = (-5)(5) + (4)(2) + (7)(4) = -25 + 8 + 28 = 11\), and their magnitudes are \(\left|\overrightarrow{DV}\right| = \sqrt{25 + 16 + 49} = \sqrt{90}\) and \(\left|\overrightarrow{DA}\right| = \sqrt{25 + 4 + 16} = \sqrt{45}\).
Since \(\sqrt{90} \times \sqrt{45} = \sqrt{4050} = 45\sqrt{2}\), we get \(\cos \angle VDA = \frac{\overrightarrow{DV} \cdot \overrightarrow{DA}}{\left|\overrightarrow{DV}\right|\left|\overrightarrow{DA}\right|} = \frac{11}{45\sqrt{2}} = \frac{11\sqrt{2}}{90}\).
Hence \(\angle VDA = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{11\sqrt{2}}{90}\right)\), which is about \(80^\circ\). (The dot product is positive, so the angle must be acute, and it is.)

rows.stem: What is the projection of vector \(\overrightarrow{DV}\) on vector \(\overrightarrow{DA}\) ?
rows.context:
An instructor at the astronomical centre shows three among the brightest stars in a particular constellation. Assume that the telescope is located at O(0, 0, 0) and the three stars have their locations at the points D, A and V having position vectors \(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\), \(7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\) and \(-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}\) respectively.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
The projection of one vector on another is their dot product divided by the magnitude of the vector being projected onto, so the projection of \(\overrightarrow{DV}\) on \(\overrightarrow{DA}\) is \(\frac{\overrightarrow{DV} \cdot \overrightarrow{DA}}{\left|\overrightarrow{DA}\right|}\).
Both vectors start at D: \(\overrightarrow{DV} = \left(-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 11\hat{k}\right) - \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\right) = -5\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}\) and \(\overrightarrow{DA} = \left(7\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\right) - \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\right) = 5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\).
Their dot product is \((-5)(5) + (4)(2) + (7)(4) = -25 + 8 + 28 = 11\), and \(\left|\overrightarrow{DA}\right| = \sqrt{25 + 4 + 16} = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\).
Hence the projection is \(\frac{11}{3\sqrt{5}} = \frac{11\sqrt{5}}{15}\) units, which is about \(1{\cdot}64\) units. (It is positive, so \(\overrightarrow{DV}\) leans towards \(\overrightarrow{DA}\) rather than away from it.)

rows.stem: What is the probability that at least one of them is selected ?
rows.context:
Rohit, Jaspreet and Alia appeared for an interview for three vacancies in the same post. The probability of Rohit's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\), Jaspreet's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) and Alia's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). The event of selection is independent of each other.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figure: DECORATIVE - a clip-art illustration of three candidates. It carries no data; all three probabilities are in the passage. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
It is quicker to work through the complement, since at least one is the opposite of none.
The three selections are independent, and the probabilities of not being selected are \(1 - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{4}{5}\) for Rohit, \(1 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}\) for Jaspreet and \(1 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}\) for Alia.
So \(P(\text{none is selected}) = \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{24}{60} = \frac{2}{5}\), and therefore \(P(\text{at least one is selected}) = 1 - \frac{2}{5} = \frac{3}{5}\).

rows.stem: Find \(P(G\,|\,\overline{H})\) where G is the event of Jaspreet's selection and \(\overline{H}\) denotes the event that Rohit is not selected.
rows.context:
Rohit, Jaspreet and Alia appeared for an interview for three vacancies in the same post. The probability of Rohit's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\), Jaspreet's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) and Alia's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). The event of selection is independent of each other.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
By the definition of conditional probability, \(P\left(G\,|\,\overline{H}\right) = \frac{P\left(G \cap \overline{H}\right)}{P\left(\overline{H}\right)}\).
The events of selection are independent, so \(P\left(G \cap \overline{H}\right) = P(G)\,P\left(\overline{H}\right) = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{4}{5} = \frac{4}{15}\), while \(P\left(\overline{H}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{4}{5}\).
Hence \(P\left(G\,|\,\overline{H}\right) = \frac{4/15}{4/5} = \frac{4}{15} \times \frac{5}{4} = \frac{1}{3}\).
This is simply \(P(G)\) over again, which is exactly what independence means: knowing that Rohit was not selected tells us nothing about Jaspreet.

rows.stem: Find the probability that exactly one of them is selected.
rows.context:
Rohit, Jaspreet and Alia appeared for an interview for three vacancies in the same post. The probability of Rohit's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\), Jaspreet's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) and Alia's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). The event of selection is independent of each other.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Write R, J and A for the events that Rohit, Jaspreet and Alia respectively are selected, so \(P(R) = \frac{1}{5}\), \(P(J) = \frac{1}{3}\), \(P(A) = \frac{1}{4}\), and the complements are \(P\left(\overline{R}\right) = \frac{4}{5}\), \(P\left(\overline{J}\right) = \frac{2}{3}\), \(P\left(\overline{A}\right) = \frac{3}{4}\).
Exactly one selected splits into three mutually exclusive cases, one for each candidate who might be the lucky one, and independence lets each be multiplied out:
\(P(R)\,P\left(\overline{J}\right)P\left(\overline{A}\right) = \frac{1}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{6}{60}\),
\(P\left(\overline{R}\right)P(J)\,P\left(\overline{A}\right) = \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{12}{60}\),
\(P\left(\overline{R}\right)P\left(\overline{J}\right)P(A) = \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{8}{60}\).
Adding the three, \(P(\text{exactly one is selected}) = \frac{6 + 12 + 8}{60} = \frac{26}{60} = \frac{13}{30}\).

rows.stem: Find the probability that exactly two of them are selected.
rows.context:
Rohit, Jaspreet and Alia appeared for an interview for three vacancies in the same post. The probability of Rohit's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\), Jaspreet's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) and Alia's selection is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). The event of selection is independent of each other.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Write R, J and A for the events that Rohit, Jaspreet and Alia respectively are selected, so \(P(R) = \frac{1}{5}\), \(P(J) = \frac{1}{3}\), \(P(A) = \frac{1}{4}\), and the complements are \(P\left(\overline{R}\right) = \frac{4}{5}\), \(P\left(\overline{J}\right) = \frac{2}{3}\), \(P\left(\overline{A}\right) = \frac{3}{4}\).
Exactly two selected splits into three mutually exclusive cases, one for each candidate who might be the one left out, and independence lets each be multiplied out:
\(P(R)\,P(J)\,P\left(\overline{A}\right) = \frac{1}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{3}{60}\),
\(P(R)\,P\left(\overline{J}\right)P(A) = \frac{1}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{2}{60}\),
\(P\left(\overline{R}\right)P(J)\,P(A) = \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{4}{60}\).
Adding the three, \(P(\text{exactly two are selected}) = \frac{3 + 2 + 4}{60} = \frac{9}{60} = \frac{3}{20}\).
